title: Decoding Corporate Earnings Reports and Earnings Season
content:
Four times a year, publicly traded companies in the United States must file detailed financial statements with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). This quarterly ritual—spanning January, April, July, and October—is known on Wall Street as 'Earnings Season.'

During earnings releases, analysts and market participants focus primarily on three core elements: revenue, earnings per share (EPS), and forward guidance.

Revenue represents the total top-line sales generated by the business. Earnings per share (EPS) represents bottom-line net profit divided by outstanding shares. Analysts formulate consensus estimates for both metrics. When a company exceeds expectations, it is termed an 'earnings beat'; when it falls short, it is an 'earnings miss.'

However, a common puzzle for beginner investors is seeing a stock plunge even after beating both revenue and earnings estimates. This paradox almost always boils down to Forward Guidance. Management's outlook for upcoming quarters is far more important to forward-looking markets than past results. If a company reports record quarterly profits but lowers revenue guidance due to slowing consumer demand, the stock often drops sharply.

Investors can inspect SEC Form 10-Q (quarterly report) and Form 10-K (annual report) on the SEC EDGAR system to evaluate revenue quality, gross margins, free cash flow generation, and debt levels directly.
